analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage lenders to verify borrowers' ability to repay and bans steering, prepayment penalties, and excessive fees.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on April 22, 2009 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written post-housing-crisis protections directly into federal lending law for home mortgages. Lenders and mortgage brokers would have had to verify, with documents like tax returns and pay stubs, that a borrower could actually afford a loan's full payments — including taxes, insurance, and a rate that could rise on adjustable loans. It would have banned brokers from steering borrowers into pricier loans than they qualified for, banned prepayment penalties, capped financed fees at 5% of the loan, imposed fiduciary duties on brokers, and required counseling before anyone refinanced certain government-subsidized mortgages.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners, particularly people taking out adjustable-rate loans or dealing with mortgage brokers. Borrowers would know before signing that their income had actually been verified against the full cost of the loan, could not be pushed into a more expensive loan than they qualified for, could pay off the loan early without a penalty, and would pay no more than 5% of the loan amount in financed fees. Homeowners with state, local, or nonprofit 'special mortgages' would get independent counseling before refinancing out of them. Small mortgage brokers would have had to meet a $500,000 net worth or $50,000 bond requirement, and borrowers would gain a legal remedy against brokers who broke the rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homebuyers and homeowners taking out mortgages

how_it_helps.text: Before making or arranging any loan secured by a borrower's home, creditors and mortgage brokers would have had to verify the borrower's reasonable ability to pay principal, interest, taxes, insurance, assessments, and mortgage insurance — using tax returns, payroll records, or bank records, with the borrower's own statement of income explicitly insufficient.

For adjustable-rate loans, ability to pay would have been measured at the fully indexed rate plus 2 percentage points with a fully amortizing schedule, and home equity could not be counted toward the borrower's ability to pay.

Brokers and creditors would have been barred from steering, counseling, or directing a consumer to rates, charges, principal amounts, or prepayment terms more expensive than those the consumer qualifies for, and from mischaracterizing credit history or appraised values.
Prepayment penalties would have been banned on all home-secured consumer loans, and financed points, charges, and fees capped at 5% of the loan principal.

Mortgage brokers would have owed borrowers fiduciary-style duties — acting in the consumer's best interest and good faith, no undisclosed compensation, disclosure of material facts — with a private cause of action letting consumers recover fees and unlawful compensation as damages.

Before refinancing a 'special mortgage' — a subsidized or soft-second loan from a state, tribal, local government, or nonprofit with borrower-friendly terms like forgivable principal or payments under 2% — the borrower would have had to get written certification from an independent HUD-certified counselor that they received counseling on the transaction's advisability.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers. They would have absorbed the cost of documented income verification on every loan, lost prepayment penalties and yield-spread-style compensation (allowed only in a narrow form with no other fees), faced a 5% cap on financed charges, owed fiduciary duties enforceable in court, and — along with anyone who bought or was assigned the loan — faced civil liability for violations. Small and mid-sized brokers would have needed $500,000 in net worth or a $50,000 bond to stay in business.

drawbacks.text: The minimum financial requirement — $500,000 in net worth or a $50,000 surety bond — would have forced many small, independent mortgage brokers out of the business, concentrating lending among large institutions and potentially reducing loan access in communities served by small brokers.

Strictly verifying income and testing affordability at a fully indexed rate plus 2 percentage points, counting taxes and insurance but not home equity, would have denied credit to some borrowers — including self-employed and lower-income buyers — who might nonetheless have managed the loan.

Requiring independent counseling before refinancing a subsidized 'special mortgage' would have added cost and delay for low-income homeowners trying to refinance out of those loans, and the assignee-liability provision could have made investors more cautious about buying mortgages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — verified ability to repay, an anti-steering duty, a prepayment-penalty ban, and a fee cap — address the exact practices that produced waves of foreclosures when borrowers were put into loans they could not afford, and the private right of action gave the rules teeth. The trade-offs are real but secondary: some borrowers at the margin would have been screened out of credit, and the broker net-worth requirement was heavy-handed, threatening small firms more than bad actors. On balance the consumer benefit outweighed the cost, though a broker-capitalization rule of that size could have been tailored better.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the Fairness for Homeowners Act of 2009 on April 22, 2009; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — and the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and brokers came out ahead: the Congress ended with none of the bill's ability-to-repay verification, anti-steering, fee-cap, fiduciary-duty, or capitalization requirements ever enacted through this bill, so the industry avoided those costs and liabilities via this route.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and a committee that never acted; no party position was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill would have banned steering borrowers into costlier loans, imposed fiduciary duties with a private right of action, capped broker compensation, and required $500,000 in net worth or a $50,000 bond to operate. Brokers' income from placing borrowers in pricier loans than they qualified for would have ended, and many small firms would have exited. Its death left that compensation model in place.

Lenders would have had to document every borrower's ability to repay, give up prepayment penalties, cap financed fees at 5% of the loan, and face liability extending to violations of the new underwriting rules. Avoiding these underwriting and liability costs is the industry's interest in the bill's failure.

The bill would have made assignees and holders of a mortgage liable in civil damages for violations of the origination rules, and let courts order loan modifications at no cost to the consumer as a remedy. The bill's death spared investors that exposure.

The bill would have required independent counseling, certified by HUD or state housing agencies, before any borrower refinanced a government-subsidized 'special mortgage,' steering business to certified nonprofits and protecting borrowers from losing favorable loan terms.
